entry.title: Andrej Karpathy says understanding of large language model capabilities is diverging sharply among different user groups [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Andrej Karpathy highlights a widening gap in how different groups perceive the capabilities of large language models (LLMs). He categorizes users into four groups: about 6 billion people with little to no exposure to LLMs, 1-2 billion casual users who see them as basic tools, around 20 million professionals using advanced LLMs for complex tasks, and roughly 5,000 insiders with access to frontier-grade systems enabling large-scale, rapid projects beyond typical human comprehension. Karpathy explains this divergence results from factors including the scale and ambition of problems tackled, the uneven development of LLM capabilities across domains like math and coding, and varying levels of access to these technologies. He notes that while the general public and many professionals experience only modest benefits, a small group is witnessing transformative impacts, creating a sharp divide in shared understanding of AI capabilities.

entry.title: Sakana AI researchers introduce Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS) for recursive self-improvement using collective intelligence in AI models [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Researchers at Sakana AI and UC Berkeley have developed Multi-Agent Self-Supervision (MASS), a method enabling AI models to recursively improve themselves by optimizing multi-agent workflows and distilling collective intelligence as a self-supervision signal. MASS uses a single language model to act as task executor, workflow optimizer, and evaluator, allowing the model to refine its own processes without external supervision, particularly on non-verifiable research tasks. The approach draws inspiration from human collective learning and scientific communities, where shared knowledge and division of labor enhance problem-solving. MASS iteratively optimizes team workflows based on self-evaluation feedback and updates the model by learning from the best-performing workflows, demonstrating improved performance on research benchmarks compared to the base model. This method aims to advance AI's capacity for continual self-learning where the model serves as both optimizer and evaluator.

entry.title: Researchers use AI agents to decompile a popular first-person shooter into readable C++ code over three months, focusing on accuracy and stability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: A team spent three months orchestrating autonomous AI agents to decompile a well-known first-person shooter game into accurate, readable C++ source code. Their goal was to recreate the game with semantic correctness, including security and bug fixes, while enabling portability across platforms like Linux and macOS. The project involved multiple AI models and tools, with agents communicating via Discord and managing progress through GitHub issues. Despite visible progress such as launching the game and loading maps, the team found that the decompiled code was semantically incorrect in places. They optimized the AI setup by reducing token consumption and maintaining agent focus through regular instruction refreshes. The effort highlighted challenges in long-term AI orchestration and the complexity of fully accurate decompilation using AI agents.

entry.title: Microsoft president says AI is less regulated than milk and calls for global safety rules including legal breach notifications and independent evaluations
entry.summary: Microsoft president Brad Smith highlighted that artificial intelligence currently faces fewer safety regulations than everyday products like milk and washing machines. He called for urgent global rules, including legal obligations to notify victims if AI systems are breached and independent evaluators to approve AI products before release. Smith emphasized the need for "emergency brakes" or kill switches to pause AI if it goes out of control and suggested the UK is well-positioned to lead these regulatory efforts due to its AI Security Institute. His views contrast with former President Donald Trump's stance favoring industry self-regulation to maintain US competitiveness.

entry.title: JulianFlux launches electrodynamic vector retrieval system using Lorentz Force equations to improve AI agent reasoning and reduce hallucinations in enterprise environments [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: JulianFlux introduces a new AI reasoning infrastructure that replaces traditional static vector databases with a dynamic electrodynamic field approach. By compressing high-dimensional embeddings into a low-rank manifold and applying physics-based routing using a modified Lorentz Force equation, the system aims to prevent hallucinations and maintain causal workflows for autonomous AI agents in enterprise settings. The open-source Python repository demonstrates key innovations including the Julian-Gauss Fast Transform for dimensionality reduction, dynamic Gaussian bandwidths adapting to semantic densities, and electric fields that repel contradictory data. The system also incorporates temporal decay of outdated information and causal momentum to guide AI agents sequentially through tasks. A Rust/CUDA backend is planned for high-frequency production use to enable sub-millisecond latency across billions of vectors.

entry.title: Researchers identify five practical AI safety problems related to unintended harmful behaviors in machine learning systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: This paper discusses the risk of accidents in AI systems, defined as unintended and harmful behaviors arising from poor design. It categorizes five key research problems: avoiding side effects, avoiding reward hacking, scalable supervision, safe exploration, and distributional shift, each linked to challenges in objective functions or learning processes. The authors review prior work and suggest research directions focused on current AI technologies, aiming to improve safety in future AI applications.

entry.title: LlamaIndex launches OpenDocRouter API to unify document parsing across multiple OCR and frontier models with layout and benchmarking features [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: LlamaIndex has introduced OpenDocRouter, a platform offering a unified API for parsing documents into markdown using a variety of open-source and frontier OCR models. The API supports PDFs, PNGs, JPEGs, and URLs, allowing synchronous or asynchronous processing with layout extraction and bounding box grounding for consistent output across models. OpenDocRouter benchmarks each model on quality and cost using ParseBench and includes models like Claude Opus 5.5, Gemini 3 Flash, GPT-6 Luna, and several open-source options. Pricing is token-based with initial credits for new users, and the platform plans to quickly integrate new models and improve popular ones. OpenDocRouter complements LlamaIndex's managed document platform, LlamaParse, by focusing on flexible model hosting and routing.

entry.title: Plimsoll launches a self-hosted sandbox to securely run AI agent-generated code with verifiable isolation levels [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Plimsoll is a self-hosted sandbox environment designed to safely execute code written by AI agents, providing developers with control over the isolation strength of each run. It reports the isolation tier achieved, ranging from process to virtual machine level, and enforces minimum isolation requirements before code execution. The tool includes features to test AI-generated code against predefined scenarios, producing cryptographic hashes as evidence of consistent behavior. It also enables secure API calls from sandboxed code without exposing credentials or network access, using a broker system that enforces permissions externally. Plimsoll aims to offer a transparent and verifiable boundary for running untrusted AI-generated code on user infrastructure.

entry.title: HPE unveils 13th generation ProLiant servers with AMD CPUs and enhanced AI capabilities for enterprise inferencing and agentic workloads, launching through 2027 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
entry.summary: Hewlett Packard Enterprise has introduced the first models of its 13th generation ProLiant servers designed to meet the growing demands of AI workloads in data centers. These systems feature AMD's latest Epyc 9006 CPUs, support for multiple GPUs, and improvements in compute, memory, and networking to handle AI inferencing, large language models, and agentic AI tasks with a focus on security and reliability. The initial offerings include the ProLiant DL585a, a 10U server supporting up to eight double-wide GPUs and dual AMD Epyc CPUs with up to 256 cores each, scheduled for release in March 2027. The ProLiant DL525, available next month, is a single-socket 1U system optimized for high data-throughput workloads like AI inference and fraud detection. HPE also plans new XD series servers with shared power and cooling for efficiency, targeting enterprise and mid-tier service providers adapting to AI's increasing infrastructure needs.

entry.title: Zuckerberg's Big Biotech Moment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: • The Big Read: Meet Zach Frankel, the secretive investor behind Cognition, Ramp • Why techies are hoarding AI compute in their homes • Plus, Recommendations-our weekly pop culture picks: "Bram Stoker's Dracula," "The AGI Chronicles" and "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" Mark Zuckerberg, the founder and CEO of Meta Platforms, was only six years old in 1990, the year the Human Genome Project got launched. That project, a multibillion-dollar international effort led by the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy, resulted in the announcement 10 years later of an awe-inspiring milestone: the first sequencing of the human genetic code-the building blocks of life. When President Bill Clinton described the achievement in 2000, he framed it in grand terms: "We are learning the language in which God created life." So it was intriguing to hear another scientific collaboration compared to that earlier achievement at a reception this week hosted by Biohub, the primary philanthropic effort of Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan. The event this week is one of a number of recent moments that herald a changing of the scientific guard from major universities to big tech companies. Speaking at the Treehouse Hotel in Sunnyvale, Calif., Zuckerberg told the gathering of around 100 tech executives, scientists and academics that he and Chan had started the first version of what is now called Biohub almost 10 years ago to the day with the goal of trying to cure and prevent all diseases by the end of the century. "We got a lot of eye rolls," Zuckerberg said. "People thought that was kind of crazy." Thanks to AI and other advances in technology, he added, "That no longer seems quite so crazy." He then turned to Lori Goler, president of the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, who announced that Biohub is partnering with the National Institutes of Health and the Department of Energy in a $1.8 billion investment to create new technologies and build the scientific infrastructure required to drive "AI-powered biology." Biohub, which launched what it calls the "Virtual Biology Initiative" in April with a $500 million commitment, also said at the event that Meta, Google DeepMind and Isomorphic Labs, a company spun off of DeepMind, have agreed to kick in $300 million. "We were inspired by the Human Genome Project," Goler told the group. Goler added that they hope the initiative "will have the same level of impact and will be as important as the Human Genome Project has been." (Anyone going to The Information's WTF Summit later this month will hear more from Goler on the future of AI biology.) Despite the evening's focus on collaboration, science can be an isolating discipline in its daily practice. When I visit labs, I am always amazed by how quiet they are. The scientists are usually intently concentrating on not making a false step that could lead to the contamination of an experiment. And yet, once the results leave the lab and reach the public, clamor often ensues. Controversial findings spark debate over ethical and moral questions. Transformative discoveries are celebrated with an element of pageantry and recognition. Both are reminders of our common humanity-and that the ultimate goal of science is to make all our lives better. This leads to invitations to the White House like the one that happened back in 2000 with the scientists at the helm of the Human Genome Project. Or even more personal celebratory videos like the ones posted on social media all this week by happy scientists who received early morning calls from Sweden learning they had won Nobel Prizes. (How can you not be moved by this video of the Stanford neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth telling his kids he won the Nobel Prize for medicine?) Zuckerberg is one of the most prominent symbols of how AI is altering the scientific landscape and bringing new leaders into an arena once dominated by major universities. He was appointed by President Trump in March to be a member of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. He is joined there by other high-profile Silicon Valley names, including Google's Sergey Brin, Oracle's Larry Ellison and Nvidia's Jensen Huang. Of the 13 people now on the council, only one is an academic researcher. Two other signs this week reflect the change. On Oct. 8, Brin and Huang, alongside other tech notables, received the National Medals of Science from President Trump. The same day, Anthropic said it is expanding its own partnership with the government. It will provide $150 million worth of AI credits and other support for the Genesis Mission launched by Trump last year to use AI to accelerate scientific discoveries. A Biohub team traveled to Washington in July to attend the first Genesis Mission Summit. Plans for the newly announced partnership with the National Institutes of Health and Department of Energy grew out of that visit. So perhaps it's only fair that the government made its own pilgrimage out to Silicon Valley. Appearing on stage together is another way of showing a shared faith that Silicon Valley and AI are the favored engines these days to try to unlock insights into the mysteries of our cells and what goes wrong when we get sick. I talked briefly with Goler the day after the reception. She said Biohub plans to host an annual AI and bio event. Biohub will likely find more guests eager to attend, from the private sector and the government. "It really is a cultural moment," she said.-Amy Dockser Marcus (amy.marcus@theinformation.com) Weekend's Latest Stories The Big Read Shroud of Secrecy Cloaks Star Investor Behind Cognition, Ramp While an air of mystery hangs around Zach Frankel, he has picked up stakes in some of tech's buzziest companies and established an extensive web of connections. The GPUs in the Wine Cellar Techies are tricking out their homes with powerful AI computers. Then come the heat issues. Listening: "Bram Stoker's Dracula" How do you give, uh, fresh life to Bram Stoker's classic? Filling it up with an all-star cast of film actors sure works. In Audible's new adaptation of "Dracula," Jonathan Bailey is the undead count; Maggie Gyllenhaal is Van Helsing, the occult expert who leads the expedition to destroy the vampire; and Ella Purnell (from "Fallout" and "Yellowjackets") is Mina, a character reimagined from Stoker's original from hapless victim into the story's central protagonist. Thanks to its Amazon budget, Audible clearly spared no expense: the sound production is top-notch and directing duties of the audio dramatization went to Mary Lambert, a Hollywood veteran best known for her 1989 film adaptation of Stephen King's "Pet Sematary." -Abram Brown Reading: "The AGI Chronicles" by Kevin Roose How exactly did we get here-to this moment in time with AIs that increasingly seem human absolutely everywhere? And that's to say nothing of the endless hand-wringing about whether they're actually going to end all of us humans. A rather definitive answer to that question lies in "The AGI Chronicles," a colorful, insidery account of the tech industry's rapacious quest to develop artificial general intelligence. Or, as author Kevin Roose terms it, "the strangest decade in our history." Roose, the former New York Times technology columnist, begins in the 2010s, a period when creating human-like AI was seen as something "between a pipe dream and a fantasy," he writes, though a few people who are now bold-faced names wanted to give it a shot: OpenAI's Sam Altman, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and Google DeepMind's Demis Hassabis among them. Of course, what looked like a quixotic endeavor then quickly morphed into the multitrillion-dollar competition that currently surrounds us. As Roose charts the twists and turns, he includes many little details to love. Just before Altman, Oracle's Larry Ellison and President Donald Trump announced Project Stargate in January 2025, Altman had to send a last-minute text message to Jeff Bezos to make sure they could use that name for their massive data center initiative: Bezos's Amazon owns MGM, and MGM owns the rights to the "Stargate" TV-and-movie franchise. Meanwhile, Google's Gemini was almost called Titan-a Hassabis suggestion-but company lawyers vetoed the name as "too aggressive." And when Daniela Amodei worked at OpenAI, she and her husband, an early OpenAI board member, used a large collection of stuffed animals as their "personal advisory council," as Roose puts it. (That detail went viral a bit last week from an early excerpt of the book.) From "The AGI Chronicles," what I was struck by most is how the AI race has warped its contestants and magnified their worst tendencies. I expect that trend will continue. It's not as if they'll be facing any less pressure anytime soon. According to Roose, many of those titans echoed the same sentiment in conversations with him-that they "missed their old lives, and they relished the times when everyone thought they were crazy for believing that AGI was possible," he writes. "Being an underdog, they said, was more fun than being a power broker, with all the scrutiny and skepticism it brought."-A.B. Watching: "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" By actor Mahershala Ali's own telling, the past few years have been challenging, with his fate skewed by other forces that have defied his control, including Marvel's decision to shelve his reboot of "Blade," its half-vampire vampire slayer. "I think in some ways I'm probably just now starting to let certain things go, because there are ways in which I think I've begun to let go of my expectations of the world and the business," Ali said in a recent GQ interview to promote his new film, "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother." "It's like you're fighting with people to see you how you see yourself." I can see how Ali's own real-life wrestling with his identity and fate might've fueled his interest in doing "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother." His character in the film, a mournful hitman named Latif, faces those same challenges-as he tries to extricate himself from a dingy Houston underworld and take up single-parent duties to his three children. Complicating that escape is a gangster pastor (John Cho) and his mobster former employer (Laith Nakli). The thriller-ish drama is punctuated by several balletic action sequences, all deftly handled by newcomer director Bassam Tariq, who'd been attached to helm the "Blade" reboot with Ali. If nothing else, "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother" is a sharp jab to Marvel's ribs: Tariq and Ali seem like they would've made a terrific "Blade" together.-A.B.

entry.title: GPUs in the Wine Cellar: Why Techies Are Hoarding AI Compute in Their Homes [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: The basement of Gary Flake's contemporary home in a quiet neighborhood in Bellevue, Wash., is furnished with everything you'd expect in a multipurpose man cave. There's a cozy-looking couch situated between a large screen and a digital projector, a Peloton treadmill and a rowing machine. The real showpiece of the space, however, is a custom computer that resembles an oversized erector set, one with seven large Nvidia graphics processing units dangling from its frame. Flake, a former Microsoft executive and startup founder, built the computer to train custom AI models on terabytes of data from electroencephalograms, the tests that measure electrical activity in the brain-part of a startup project he has since moved on from. To train his AI models, Flake could have paid a cloud service to train them on the industrial-strength GPUs inside their data centers, but he said it was far cheaper to assemble his own machine out of discounted parts (total cost: under $6,000) than to fork over fees to Amazon Web Services or Microsoft every month. That's true even when including the $10,000 to $20,000 he spent for electrical upgrades and a new HVAC system he bought to keep his basement cool while his AI computer throws off a lot of heat. "I want to own," said Flake, who plans to begin using the computer again for a new AI project in the coming months. "I don't want to rent."

entry.title: China's AI Model Race Is Just Getting More Crowded [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
entry.summary: Imagine Epic Games, Apple and DoorDash were developing their own large language models now from scratch to compete against the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic. That's basically what's happening in China, where a trio of big names from other parts of the tech industry have jumped into an already-crowded race to make cutting-edge AI. MiHoYo, a Shanghai-based videogame maker behind such hits like Genshin Impact, is developing its own LLMs with the goal of becoming a top-tier lab in China in the next couple of years. Xiaomi, a leading smartphone maker that also sells electric cars, released its latest LLM two weeks ago. And Meituan, China's biggest food delivery and local services app, in June unveiled a more powerful version of the LLM it launched last year.
